title: Hallucination taxonomy
summary: Hallucination is not one bug. Splitting it into factuality versus faithfulness, and intrinsic versus extrinsic, tells you which control to apply and how to detect it.
useIf: You must diagnose a wrong answer, choose mitigations, or design evals that separate unsupported claims from false ones.
avoidIf: You treat it as one defect to patch with a prompt line such as 'do not make things up'.

explain.md: Huang et al. split LLM hallucination into **factuality** (output conflicts with real-world facts) and **faithfulness** (output is inconsistent with instructions, supplied context or its own logic), with causes in data, training and inference [[r43]]. The older natural-language-generation split is **intrinsic** (the output contradicts the source) versus **extrinsic** (the output cannot be verified from the source) [[r43]]. In a RAG system the source is the retrieved context, so these two views give you a decision path. Route fixes by type: missing knowledge points to grounding, ignored context points to faithfulness controls and fabricated support points to citation checks.

explain.title: Classify a suspicious claim
explain.alt: A decision tree. If a claim contradicts the provided context it is intrinsic. If it is absent from the context and unverifiable it is extrinsic. If supported by context, check whether the source is true in the world.
explain.src:
flowchart TD
  A[Claim in the answer] --> B{Supported by the provided context?}
  B -->|Contradicts it| C[Intrinsic, faithfulness]
  B -->|Not in it| D[Extrinsic, unverifiable]
  B -->|Supported| E{True in the world?}
  E -->|No| F[Source error]
  E -->|Yes| G[Grounded]

explain.md: **Why it persists.** The 2025-09 paper *Why Language Models Hallucinate* argues errors resemble binary classification mistakes, and that benchmarks that reward guessing over abstaining keep them alive [[r44]]. That makes hallucination partly an **incentive problem**. Your controls should include abstention paths, evals that score a confident error worse than 'I do not know', unanswerable questions in the test set and citation checks, not only a stronger model.

whereToUse: Triage of wrong answers: label each failure by type before picking a fix
Designing RAG evals that separate retrieval gaps, unsupported claims and false sources
Setting abstention and citation policies for assistants in regulated domains
Writing groundedness and fact-check judges with distinct rubrics
Interview answers that explain mitigations by cause, not by slogan

use: Label failures as factuality, faithfulness, intrinsic or extrinsic before changing anything
Pair each type with its control and its detector
avoid: Treating one prompt line as the mitigation
Scoring answers so that 'I do not know' always loses
Judging groundedness without the retrieved context in front of the judge
flips: No context is supplied (open chat): factuality dominates, so add retrieval or web grounding
Context is supplied: faithfulness dominates, so enforce citations and claim checks
Stakes rise: raise the abstention threshold and add human review

pitfalls.symptom: The model gives a confident answer when evidence is missing
pitfalls.cause: Training and benchmarks reward guessing over abstaining
pitfalls.fix: Evaluate so abstention beats a confident error, include unanswerable questions and require citations.

pitfalls.symptom: An answer contradicts the supplied document
pitfalls.cause: A faithfulness failure: the context was overridden by prior knowledge or ignored
pitfalls.fix: Cite per claim, check claims against retrieved text and tighten instructions to answer only from context.

pitfalls.symptom: Citations look right but do not support the claim
pitfalls.cause: The model attached plausible links without verification
pitfalls.fix: Verify each claim against the cited span and treat unverifiable citations as failures.

scenarios.title: RAG answer contradicts the policy document
scenarios.situation: A policy assistant retrieves the right passage but its answer says the opposite of what the passage states. Users trust it, and wrong answers carry moderate risk.
constraints: Latency budget allows one extra check
unknowns: Do prompts say to answer only from context?
scenarios.question: Which fix first?

options.name: Swap to a bigger model
options.why: The failure is a context contradiction, not missing knowledge, and size does not guarantee faithfulness.
options.tradeoff: Right if a weak model cannot follow the context at all.

options.name: Add more retrieval documents
options.why: More evidence can help borderline cases.
options.tradeoff: The right passage was already present, so this adds noise and cost.

options.name: Require per-claim citations and run an NLI-style check of claims against the passage
options.why: It targets intrinsic faithfulness failures and gives you a detector for evals.
options.tradeoff: Extra latency and some false positives that need tuning.

flips.if: The check adds too much latency
flips.then: Run it asynchronously on a sample and alert, and keep a sync check only for high-risk answers.
Block or escalate answers that fail the check.

scenarios.takeaway: Contradiction of supplied text calls for claim-level checks, not a bigger model.

scenarios.title: Open-domain Q and A with no documents
scenarios.situation: A public assistant answers general questions with no retrieval. It sometimes states wrong dates and invents references.
unknowns: Can the assistant call a search tool?
scenarios.question: What is the best mitigation?

options.name: Add 'do not hallucinate' to the system prompt
options.why: The 2025 analysis frames hallucination as partly a training and incentive problem, and a sentence does not change what the model knows.
options.tradeoff: Fine as a minor hint beside real controls.

options.name: Add retrieval or web grounding, allow abstention and verify cited sources
options.why: It addresses factuality by supplying evidence and permits 'I do not know'.
options.tradeoff: Search latency and the need to vet sources.

options.name: Fine-tune on a set of correct facts
options.tradeoff: Does not cover unseen facts and becomes stale.

flips.if: Stakes are low and speed matters
flips.then: Allow ungrounded answers with a visible confidence label.

scenarios.takeaway: Factuality gaps need evidence and permission to abstain.

scenarios.title: Evals that punish refusals
scenarios.situation: An internal eval gives full credit for any correct answer and zero for 'I do not know'. Teams tune prompts to avoid refusals and complain of confident errors in production.
constraints: Unanswerable questions exist in real traffic
unknowns: What share of real questions is unanswerable?
What does a wrong answer cost?
scenarios.question: What do you change?

options.name: Rescore so a confident error is worse than abstaining, and add unanswerable cases
options.why: The 2025 analysis says benchmarks that reward guessing keep hallucination alive, so fix the incentive in your own evals.
options.tradeoff: Refusal rates may rise at first and need calibration.

options.name: Remove the 'I do not know' option from the UX
options.why: It forces guessing and makes confident errors more likely.
options.tradeoff: Only fine if a human always reviews the output.

options.name: Lower the temperature
options.tradeoff: Does not change the incentive to guess, so confident errors remain.

flips.if: Wrong answers are cheap and refusals are costly

flips.then: Weight confident errors even more heavily.

scenarios.takeaway: Hallucination is partly an evaluation incentive problem.

quiz.q: Match each term to its meaning.

pairs.r: Output is inconsistent with instructions or context
Output cannot be verified from the source

quiz.explain: Huang et al. use factuality and faithfulness. The older NLG terms intrinsic and extrinsic describe contradiction versus unverifiable content relative to the source.

quiz.q: An answer includes a claim that appears nowhere in the retrieved passages and cannot be verified from them. Which type is it?
quiz.explain: A claim that cannot be verified from the source is extrinsic. Intrinsic would contradict the passage. Tokenization is unrelated, and an unverifiable claim is not automatically a valid inference.

quiz.q: Which eval design keeps confident errors alive, according to the 2025-09 paper?
options: Scoring that rewards guessing over abstaining
Adding unanswerable questions to the test set
Per-claim citation checks on each answer
Penalizing confident errors more than abstentions
quiz.explain: The paper argues benchmarks that reward guessing over abstaining keep errors alive. The other options are mitigations.

flashcards.back: Factuality: output conflicts with real-world facts. Faithfulness: output is inconsistent with instructions, supplied context or its own logic.
Intrinsic contradicts the source. Extrinsic cannot be verified from the source. Control extrinsic claims with a citation per claim.

flashcards.front: Why do benchmarks keep hallucination alive?
flashcards.back: They reward guessing over abstaining, so models learn to guess. Fix evals so a confident error scores worse than abstaining.
